chunks: What you can do with timers. The question: What can you do with timers?
A timer can do four kinds of jobs, all in hardware. It can make things happen on a schedule, such as a regular signal to the processor or a PWM signal.
It can measure time, such as how long a pulse lasts. It can count pulses from outside. And it can trigger other parts, such as starting a measurement.
Picture a kitchen timer that has been upgraded. As an alarm, it rings every minute on schedule.
As a lap timer, you press a button when a runner crosses a line, and it records the exact time, even if you were busy. As a tally clicker, it counts how many people walk past.
As a switch, it turns a lamp on for part of each second.
One counter, four families of use.
Notice that the same counter register serves all of them; what differs is which event (overflow, compare match or edge) you hook to a pin, flag or trigger.
PWM (pulse-width modulation): switching a pin on and off repeatedly, so the average power depends on how long it stays on.
Duty cycle: the fraction of each period that the pin is on. 25% means on for a quarter of the time.
Input capture: saving the counter value at the instant an input signal switches level, to timestamp it exactly.
A hobby servo wants a pulse every 20 milliseconds, which is 50 hertz, and the pulse width sets its angle.
With the counter ticking once per microsecond (1 megahertz), set the period to 20,000 counts. Switching the pin off at count 1500 makes the pulse 1.
5 milliseconds wide, the centered position. The duty cycle is 1500 over 20000 equals 7. 5 % . Now the other direction: an ultrasonic sensor sends back an echo pulse.
Input capture records when the pulse starts and ends, to one tick, 1 microseconds. A 10 milliseconds echo means the target is 343 times 0. 010 over 2 about 1. 7 m away.
That is the whole idea.
"Timers let you generate, measure and count in hardware.
Generate: periodic interrupts for a system tick or ADC sampling, and output compare for PWM, servo pulses or one-shot strobes.
Measure: input capture timestamps an edge with one-tick resolution, so I can time an echo or tach pulse.
Count: clock the timer from a pin to count pulses or run a quadrature encoder. Plus watchdog and RTC variants.
It's all deterministic and runs without the CPU, which is why I prefer it over software delays."
